solution.why_others_wrong: 4F takes only the change in terminal velocity. 2F takes only the factor r in 6πηrv and forgets that v_t changes. 16F multiplies r² by r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', viscosity (Stokes' law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water rises to a height h in a clean glass capillary tube of radius r when the tube stands in a vessel at rest on the ground. A capillary tube of radius r/2, of the same glass, is placed in the same water inside a lift that is accelerating upward with acceleration g. The height to which the water rises in it is:

solution.concept: Capillary rise in an accelerating frame
solution.explanation: h = 2S cos θ/(ρ g_eff r). Halving the radius doubles the rise, but in a lift accelerating upward at g the effective gravity is g + g = 2g, which halves it again.
steps: h' = 2S cos θ/(ρ(2g)(r/2)) = 2S cos θ/(ρgr) = h
solution.why_others_wrong: 2h ignores the lift's acceleration. 4h treats the effective gravity as g/2. h/2 ignores the change in radius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface tension (capillary rise)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water flows steadily through a pipe that rises as it goes. At a lower section the water moves at 1 m/s; at an upper section, 2 m higher, the cross-sectional area of the pipe is half that of the lower section. Treating water as non-viscous and incompressible (density 1000 kg/m³) and taking g = 10 m/s², the pressure at the lower section exceeds that at the upper section by:

solution.concept: Equation of continuity with Bernoulli's equation
solution.explanation: Continuity (Av constant) gives the speed in the narrow upper section. Bernoulli's equation then balances pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume and potential energy per unit volume between the two sections.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁴ Pa ignores the change in speed. 1.5 × 10³ Pa ignores the rise in height. 1.85 × 10⁴ Pa subtracts the kinetic term instead of adding it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', streamline flow and Bernoulli's principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: 100 g of water at 20 °C and 100 g of ice at −20 °C are mixed in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. Take the specific heat capacity of water as 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, that of ice as 0.5 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and the latent heat of fusion of ice as 80 cal g⁻¹. When equilibrium is reached:

options.text: The temperature is 0 °C and 25 g of the ice has melted
The temperature is 0 °C and none of the ice has melted
The temperature is 0 °C and 12.5 g of the ice has melted
All the ice has melted and the temperature is above 0 °C

solution.concept: Calorimetry with partial melting
solution.explanation: First compare the heat the water can give out in cooling to 0 °C with the heat the ice needs to warm up to 0 °C. Any heat left over melts ice at 0 °C; if it cannot melt all the ice, the mixture stays at 0 °C.
steps: Remaining 1000 cal melts 1000/80 = 12.5 g of ice
Final state: 0 °C, 112.5 g water and 87.5 g ice
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 g forgets the heat needed to warm the ice to 0 °C. 'None melted' assumes the warming uses up all the heat. Melting all 100 g would need 8000 cal more than is available.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', calorimetry and change of state
solution.final_answer: Option C: The temperature is 0 °C and 12.5 g of the ice has melted

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the modes of heat transfer are correct?

(a) In conduction, heat passes between neighbouring parts of a body without any bulk motion of the material.
(b) In natural convection, gravity plays an essential part: the warmer, less dense fluid rises and the cooler, denser fluid sinks.
(c) In forced convection, the fluid is made to move by a pump, a fan or some other physical means.
(d) Heat can be transferred through a vacuum by conduction but not by radiation.
(e) Gases are poor conductors of heat compared with metals.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Conduction, convection and radiation
solution.explanation: Conduction passes energy between adjacent parts by molecular collisions (and free electrons in metals) without bulk flow. Convection needs bulk flow of a fluid: natural convection is driven by buoyancy, which needs gravity, and forced convection by a pump or fan. Radiation needs no medium; conduction does.
steps: (d) false: it is the other way round
solution.why_others_wrong: Every option except D includes the false statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A load W hung from a uniform wire of length L stretches it by x. The same wire is folded at its middle into two equal strands, each of length L/2, and the same load W is hung from the folded wire so that it is shared equally by the two strands. Within the elastic limit, the extension now is:

solution.concept: Extension of a wire, ΔL = WL/(AY)
solution.explanation: Folding halves the length of wire that is stretched and doubles the cross-sectional area that carries the load (each strand carries W/2). Both changes reduce the extension.
solution.why_others_wrong: x/2 accounts for only one of the two changes (length or area). x assumes no change. 2x doubles instead of halving.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Young's modulus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the first law of thermodynamics written as ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW, as in NCERT, the quantities ΔQ and ΔW are taken as positive when:

options.text: Heat is given out by the system, and work is done by the system on its surroundings
Heat is supplied to the system, and work is done on the system by its surroundings
Heat is supplied to the system, and work is done by the system on its surroundings
Heat is given out by the system, and work is done on the system by its surroundings

solution.concept: Sign convention in the first law
solution.explanation: ΔQ is the heat supplied to the system and ΔW the work done by the system. Heat supplied either raises the internal energy or is used by the system to do work on its surroundings.
steps: ΔQ > 0: heat flows into the system
ΔW > 0: the system does work (for example, a gas expands)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options reverse the sign convention for heat, for work, or for both.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics
solution.final_answer: Option C: Heat is supplied to the system, and work is done by the system on its surroundings

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Five moles of an ideal diatomic gas, whose molecules are rigid (no vibration), are heated in a closed rigid vessel so that the temperature rises by 20 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat supplied to the gas is:

solution.concept: Heat at constant volume, Q = nC_vΔT
solution.explanation: In a rigid vessel no work is done, so all the heat goes into internal energy. For a rigid diatomic gas C_v = (5/2)R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2905 J uses C_p = 7R/2, which applies at constant pressure. 1245 J uses the monatomic value 3R/2. 830 J uses R alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', specific heat capacity; first law of thermodynamics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas absorbs 250 J of heat while it expands at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from a volume of 1 L to 2 L. The increase in its internal energy and the ratio of its specific heats γ = C_p/C_v are respectively:

solution.concept: First law at constant pressure; Q = nC_pΔT and ΔU = nC_vΔT
solution.explanation: The work done by the gas is PΔV. The first law gives ΔU. At constant pressure the heat is nC_pΔT and the change in internal energy is nC_vΔT, so their ratio is γ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 350 J adds the work to the heat (wrong sign), giving 5/7. 3/5 is ΔU/Q, the inverse of γ. 7/5 assumes a diatomic gas without using the data.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics and specific heat capacity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On a P–V diagram, an isothermal curve and a reversible adiabatic curve of an ideal diatomic gas (rigid molecules, γ = 7/5) pass through the same point. The ratio of the slope of the adiabatic curve to that of the isothermal curve at that point is:

solution.concept: Slopes of isothermal and adiabatic curves
solution.explanation: Differentiate PV = constant and PV^γ = constant. The isothermal slope is dP/dV = −P/V and the adiabatic slope is dP/dV = −γP/V, so at the same point the adiabatic curve is steeper by the factor γ.
steps: Isothermal: P dV + V dP = 0 → dP/dV = −P/V
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/7 inverts the ratio; the adiabatic curve is the steeper one. 1 says the curves have equal slopes. 5/3 is γ for a monatomic gas.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', isothermal and adiabatic processes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a closed system, Q is the heat supplied to the system and W the work done by the system. Match List-I (values of Q and W in one process) with List-II (the change ΔU in its internal energy).

List-I:
A. Q = +100 J, W = +40 J
B. Q = −50 J, W = −80 J
C. Q = 0, W = +50 J
D. Q = +120 J, W = +200 J

List-II:
I. −80 J
II. +60 J
III. −50 J
IV. +30 J

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Applying ΔU = Q − W with signs
solution.explanation: With heat supplied to the system and work done by it both counted as positive, ΔU = Q − W.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes add W instead of subtracting it in case B, or interchange the two negative results.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two moles of an ideal diatomic gas (rigid molecules, C_v = 5R/2) at 300 K are heated at constant pressure until the temperature is 600 K. The gas then expands reversibly and adiabatically until its temperature falls back to 300 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the total work done by the gas in the two processes is:

solution.concept: Work in isobaric and adiabatic processes
solution.explanation: In the isobaric step W = nRΔT. In the adiabatic step no heat flows, so the work done equals the fall in internal energy, nC_vΔT.
steps: Check: the net ΔU is zero, so W equals the heat absorbed, nC_pΔT = 17 430 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.98 kJ counts only the isobaric step and 12.45 kJ only the adiabatic step. 7.47 kJ subtracts the two works although the gas expands, doing positive work, in both steps.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermodynamic processes (isobaric and adiabatic)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When an ideal gas is taken from an equilibrium state A to another equilibrium state B, the heat it absorbs is the same whatever path it follows.
Reason (R): The change in the internal energy of an ideal gas in going from state A to state B is the same for every path.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: State functions and path functions
solution.explanation: Internal energy is a state variable, so ΔU between A and B is fixed. The work done, the area under the P–V path, depends on the path, and therefore so does Q = ΔU + W.
steps: ΔU(A → B) is path-independent → R true
W depends on the path → Q = ΔU + W depends on the path → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C, which need A to be true, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', heat, internal energy and work; first law of thermodynamics
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the root mean square speed of hydrogen molecules (molar mass 2 g/mol) at 300 K is about:

solution.concept: rms speed, v_rms = √(3RT/M)
solution.explanation: The molar mass must be in kg/mol: M = 2 × 10⁻³ kg/mol.
solution.why_others_wrong: 61 m/s keeps the molar mass in g/mol. 1.12 km/s leaves out the factor 3. 3.7 × 10⁶ m/s forgets to take the square root.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', kinetic interpretation of temperature

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The molar specific heat at constant volume of an ideal gas of rigid diatomic molecules is 3R/2.
Reason (R): A rigid diatomic molecule has three translational and two rotational degrees of freedom.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Specific heat from the law of equipartition
solution.explanation: Each quadratic degree of freedom contributes ½k_BT per molecule, i.e. ½RT per mole. With 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom, U = (5/2)RT per mole, so C_v = 5R/2. The value 3R/2 belongs to a monatomic gas.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so A, B and C are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy and specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
One mole of each ideal gas is at absolute temperature T, and vibrations are not excited. Using the law of equipartition of energy, match List-I (energy) with List-II (its value; R is the gas constant).

List-I:
A. Total translational kinetic energy of a monatomic gas
B. Total rotational kinetic energy of a diatomic gas
C. Total kinetic energy of a diatomic gas
D. Internal energy of a gas of non-linear polyatomic molecules

List-II:
I. RT
II. 3RT
III. 3RT/2
IV. 5RT/2

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Law of equipartition of energy
solution.explanation: Each degree of freedom carries ½RT per mole. A monatomic molecule has 3 translational degrees of freedom, a rigid diatomic one adds 2 rotational, and a rigid non-linear polyatomic one has 3 rotational.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes give the diatomic molecule 3 rotational degrees of freedom or count only translation for the total.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic energies of its molecules; there is no potential energy of interaction between the molecules.
Statement II: The internal energy of a given mass of an ideal gas increases when it is compressed isothermally.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature
solution.explanation: Molecules of an ideal gas do not interact except during collisions, so the internal energy is entirely kinetic and, by equipartition, depends only on the temperature. In an isothermal compression the temperature, and hence the internal energy, stays the same.
steps: Statement I: no intermolecular forces → U is purely kinetic (true)
Statement II: T constant → U constant (false)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II would need intermolecular potential energy that depends on volume, which an ideal gas does not have; so A, B and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', molecular nature of matter and kinetic theory of an ideal gas
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two identical vessels connected by a narrow tube of negligible volume contain an ideal gas at 300 K and pressure P. One vessel is then heated to 600 K while the other is kept at 300 K. The pressure of the gas in the vessels becomes:

solution.concept: Ideal gas equation with a fixed total amount of gas
solution.explanation: The total number of moles stays the same, and when equilibrium is reached the pressure is the same in both vessels. Write n = PV/(RT) for each vessel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3P/2 uses the average temperature (450 K) for the whole gas, which is not how moles are shared. 2P assumes the gas in the heated vessel keeps its moles. P ignores the heating.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', behaviour of gases (ideal gas equation)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A vessel open to the atmosphere contains air at 27 °C. It is heated slowly, the pressure inside staying equal to the atmospheric pressure, until one-quarter of the air that was in the vessel has escaped. Neglecting the expansion of the vessel and treating air as an ideal gas, the temperature of the air in the vessel is now:

solution.concept: Ideal gas equation with escaping gas (P and V fixed)
solution.explanation: With P and V fixed, PV = nRT gives nT = constant: as the gas is heated, the amount remaining in the vessel falls in inverse proportion to the absolute temperature.
solution.why_others_wrong: 102 °C (375 K) multiplies T by 5/4 instead of 4/3. 36 °C applies the ratio to the Celsius temperature. 400 °C confuses kelvin with degrees Celsius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', behaviour of gases (ideal gas equation)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The bulk modulus of water is 2.25 × 10⁹ Pa and its density is 1000 kg/m³. The speed of sound (longitudinal waves) in water is:

solution.concept: Speed of longitudinal waves in a fluid
solution.explanation: For longitudinal waves in a fluid, v = √(B/ρ), where B is the bulk modulus.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.25 × 10⁶ m/s forgets the square root. About 47 m/s takes the density as 10⁶ kg/m³ instead of 10³ kg/m³. About 4.7 × 10⁴ m/s takes the density as 1 (its value in g/cm³).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', speed of a longitudinal wave (speed of sound)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The acceleration a of a particle is related to its displacement x by a = −16π²x, with a in m/s² and x in metres. The frequency of its oscillation is:

solution.concept: Defining relation of SHM, a = −ω²x
solution.explanation: Comparing with a = −ω²x gives ω² = 16π², so ω = 4π rad/s and ν = ω/2π.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4π is the angular frequency in rad/s, not the frequency in Hz. 0.5 Hz is the period in seconds read as a frequency. 8 Hz divides ω² by 2π².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion and uniform circular motion (a = −ω²x)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For a particle executing simple harmonic motion x = A sin ωt, the phase difference between its velocity and its acceleration is:

solution.concept: Phase relations in SHM
solution.explanation: v = Aω cos ωt and a = −Aω² sin ωt = Aω² cos(ωt + π/2). The acceleration leads the velocity by π/2: when the speed is greatest (at the mean position) the acceleration is zero, and vice versa.
steps: a = Aω² cos(ωt + π/2) → phase difference π/2
solution.why_others_wrong: π is the phase difference between displacement and acceleration. Zero would make velocity and acceleration greatest together. π/4 has no basis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The time interval between two successive maxima of sound intensity is:

solution.concept: Beat frequency and beat period
solution.explanation: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies, and the interval between successive maxima is its reciprocal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 s takes the beat frequency itself as the time. 0.5 s halves the beat frequency. About 0.004 s is the period of either fork.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', beats

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle executes simple harmonic motion x = A sin(ωt + φ). At t = 0 it is at x = +A/2 and moving towards the positive extreme position x = +A. The value of φ is:

solution.concept: Phase constant from the initial position and direction of motion
solution.explanation: At t = 0, x = A sin φ and v = Aω cos φ. The position fixes sin φ; the direction of motion fixes the sign of cos φ.
steps: A sin φ = A/2 → φ = π/6 or 5π/6
Moving towards +A → v > 0 → cos φ > 0 → φ = π/6
solution.why_others_wrong: 5π/6 also gives x = A/2 but with the particle moving towards the mean position (v < 0). π/3 gives x = A sin 60° ≈ 0.87A. π/2 puts the particle at the extreme.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion (phase)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A simple pendulum has a period T for small oscillations when it hangs in a car at rest. The car now moves on a level road with a constant acceleration of √3 g. The period of small oscillations of the pendulum about its new equilibrium position becomes:

solution.concept: Pendulum with an effective gravity
solution.explanation: In the accelerating car the bob's equilibrium is tilted; the effective gravity is the vector combination of g (down) and the car's acceleration (horizontal): g_eff = √(g² + a²). The period is 2π√(L/g_eff).
solution.why_others_wrong: T/2 forgets the square root. T assumes a horizontal acceleration does not affect the pendulum. √2 T inverts the effect: a larger effective gravity shortens the period.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', the simple pendulum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle executes simple harmonic motion with amplitude A. When its displacement from the mean position is A/2, the ratio of its kinetic energy to its potential energy is:

solution.concept: Energy at a displacement in SHM
solution.explanation: The potential energy is ½kx² and the total energy is ½kA². The kinetic energy is the difference.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 1 happens at x = A/√2, not A/2. 1 : 3 inverts the ratio. 2 : 1 takes the energies as proportional to x rather than x².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', energy in simple harmonic motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A block hanging from a light vertical spring oscillates with the same period as when the same block, attached to the same spring, oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface.
Reason (R): Gravity increases the force constant of a spring that hangs vertically.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Spring–block period is independent of gravity
solution.explanation: For the hanging block, gravity only shifts the equilibrium position (to an extension mg/k). About that position the net restoring force is still −kx, so T = 2π√(m/k) in both cases. The force constant is a property of the spring and is not changed by gravity.
steps: Vertical: net force about the new equilibrium = −kx → T = 2π√(m/k) (A true)
k does not depend on gravity (R false)
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so A and B are wrong; A is true, so D is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', oscillations due to a spring
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a stationary wave on a stretched string, the amplitude of oscillation differs from point to point, being zero at the nodes.
Statement II: In a sinusoidal progressive wave travelling along a string without loss of energy, every particle of the string oscillates with the same amplitude.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Amplitude in stationary and progressive waves
solution.explanation: A stationary wave y = 2a sin kx cos ωt has the position-dependent amplitude 2a sin kx, zero at the nodes and 2a at the antinodes. In a progressive wave y = a sin(kx − ωt), every particle has amplitude a; only the phase differs from point to point.
steps: Progressive: amplitude a everywhere (Statement II true)
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', displacement relation in a progressive wave; standing waves
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The displacement of a particle is x = 0.05 sin(10t + π/6), where x is in metres and t in seconds. Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (its value).

List-I:
A. Period of the motion
B. Maximum speed
C. Maximum magnitude of acceleration
D. Displacement at t = 0

List-II:
I. 5 m s⁻²
II. 0.025 m
III. π/5 s
IV. 0.5 m s⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Reading an SHM equation
solution.explanation: Compare with x = A sin(ωt + φ): A = 0.05 m, ω = 10 rad/s, φ = π/6. Then T = 2π/ω, v_max = Aω and a_max = Aω².
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the maximum speed with the maximum acceleration, or the period with the initial displacement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A horizontal platform moves up and down in simple harmonic motion with a frequency of (5/π) Hz. A small block rests on it. Taking g = 10 m/s², the largest amplitude of the motion for which the block never loses contact with the platform is:

solution.concept: Losing contact in vertical SHM
solution.explanation: The block stays in contact only while the normal force is positive: N = m(g − a), where a is the platform's downward acceleration. The largest downward acceleration, ω²A, occurs at the top of the motion, so we need ω²A ≤ g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 m uses g/ω instead of g/ω². 20 cm allows a downward acceleration of 2g. 1 cm has an error of a factor of 10 in ω².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two small sources of sound S₁ and S₂ vibrate in phase with the same frequency of 170 Hz. A point P is 3.0 m from S₁ and 4.5 m from S₂, and the waves from the two sources reach P with the same amplitude a. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the amplitude of the resultant oscillation at P is:

solution.concept: Superposition of two waves with a phase difference
solution.explanation: The path difference gives a phase difference φ = 2π(Δx)/λ. Two oscillations of equal amplitude a and phase difference φ combine to give amplitude 2a|cos(φ/2)|.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 needs a path difference of an odd number of half-wavelengths (φ = π, 3π, …); 1.5 m is three-quarters of a wavelength. 2a needs a whole number of wavelengths. a corresponds to φ = 2π/3.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', the principle of superposition of waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A pipe 17 cm long is closed at one end and open at the other. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s and neglecting end corrections, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its fundamental frequency is 500 Hz.
(b) The next higher frequency at which it resonates is 1500 Hz.
(c) It cannot resonate at 1000 Hz.
(d) If its closed end is opened, its fundamental frequency becomes 1000 Hz.
(e) There is a displacement antinode at its closed end.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Normal modes of closed and open pipes
solution.explanation: A pipe closed at one end has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, …: only odd harmonics v/4L, 3v/4L, … occur. A pipe open at both ends has fundamental v/2L.
steps: (c) 1000 Hz = 2f₁, an even harmonic, is absent (true)
(e) the closed end is a displacement node (false)
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) reverses node and antinode; (b), (c) and (d) only leaves out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves in pipes (closed and open)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A block of mass 1 kg attached to a light spring of force constant 100 N/m oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface with an amplitude of 0.2 m. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The angular frequency of the oscillation is 10 rad/s.
(b) The maximum speed of the block is 2 m/s.
(c) The total mechanical energy of the oscillation is 4 J.
(d) When the displacement is 0.1 m, the speed of the block is √3 m/s.
(e) The maximum magnitude of the force on the block is 20 N.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Spring–block oscillator: frequency, speed, energy and force
solution.explanation: ω = √(k/m); the speed at displacement x is ω√(A² − x²); the total energy is ½kA²; the restoring force is greatest, kA, at the extremes.
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) forgets the ½ in ½kA²; every option with (c) is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', oscillations due to a spring and energy in SHM

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric dipole of dipole moment 2 × 10⁻⁸ C m is placed in a uniform electric field of 5 × 10³ N/C, with its dipole moment at 60° to the field. Taking the potential energy to be zero when the dipole is perpendicular to the field, its potential energy is:

solution.concept: Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field, U = −pE cos θ
solution.explanation: With zero potential energy at θ = 90°, the potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field is U = −p·E = −pE cos θ.
solution.why_others_wrong: +5 × 10⁻⁵ J drops the minus sign. −8.7 × 10⁻⁵ J uses sin θ, which belongs in the torque. −1 × 10⁻⁴ J is the value for θ = 0.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential energy of a dipole in an external field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A large, thin, plane sheet carries a uniform surface charge density of 8.85 × 10⁻⁹ C/m². Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the magnitude of the electric field near the sheet, away from its edges, is:

solution.concept: Field of an infinite plane sheet of charge
solution.explanation: Applying Gauss's law to a cylinder that pierces the sheet, the flux leaves through both flat faces: 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of the distance from the sheet.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1000 N/C is σ/ε₀, the field just outside a charged conductor. 250 N/C divides by 4ε₀. 2000 N/C multiplies instead of dividing by 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', applications of Gauss's law (field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The quantisation of electric charge, first suggested by the laws of electrolysis, was demonstrated experimentally in 1912 by:

solution.concept: Quantisation of charge
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that the laws of electrolysis found by Faraday first suggested that charge is quantised, and that Millikan demonstrated it experimentally in 1912 (the oil-drop experiment).
solution.why_others_wrong: Faraday's electrolysis laws only suggested quantisation. Coulomb measured the force between charges. Thomson's work is not what NCERT credits for this demonstration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', basic properties of electric charge (quantisation of charge)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A proton is released from rest in a uniform electric field of 1 × 10⁴ N/C. Taking the charge of a proton as 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, its kinetic energy after it has moved 1 cm along the field is:

solution.concept: Work done by a uniform field on a charge
solution.explanation: The field does work qEd on the proton, which becomes its kinetic energy (work–energy theorem). Equivalently the proton falls through a potential difference Ed = 100 V and gains 100 eV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ J leaves the distance in centimetres. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is just the charge, or 1 eV. 8 × 10⁻¹⁸ J puts in an unwanted factor ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', electrostatic potential and potential difference

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A particle of charge q and mass m is in a uniform electric field E; no other force acts on it. It moves through a distance d along the field. Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (expression).

List-I:
A. Force on the particle
B. Acceleration of the particle
C. Work done by the field over the distance d
D. Potential difference between the starting and the end point

List-II:
I. Ed
II. qEd
III. qE
IV. qE/m

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Charge in a uniform electric field
solution.explanation: F = qE; a = F/m; the work done by a constant force along its own direction is Fd; and in a uniform field the potential falls by E per unit distance along the field, so the potential difference is Ed.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse work (qEd, energy) with potential difference (Ed, energy per unit charge), or force with acceleration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', electric field; 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', relation between field and potential
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel is greater than the largest of the individual capacitances.
Statement II: The equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected in series is less than the smallest of the individual capacitances.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Combination of capacitors
solution.explanation: In parallel, C = C₁ + C₂ + …, a sum of positive terms, so it exceeds each term. In series, 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + … exceeds each 1/Cᵢ, so C is smaller than every Cᵢ.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', combination of capacitors
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Electric flux of 8 × 10³ N m² C⁻¹ enters a closed surface and flux of 4 × 10³ N m² C⁻¹ leaves it. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the net charge enclosed by the surface is:

solution.concept: Gauss's law with inward and outward flux
solution.explanation: Outward flux is positive and inward flux negative. Gauss's law gives q_enclosed = ε₀ × (net outward flux).
steps: Net outward flux = 4 × 10³ − 8 × 10³ = −4 × 10³ N m² C⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: +3.54 × 10⁻⁸ C has the sign reversed: more flux enters than leaves, so the enclosed charge is negative. The 1.06 × 10⁻⁷ C options add the two fluxes instead of subtracting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', electric flux and Gauss's law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a hydrogen atom, treat the electron and the proton as point charges 0.53 Å apart. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and the potential energy to be zero at infinite separation, the electrostatic potential energy of the pair is about:

solution.concept: Potential energy of two point charges
solution.explanation: U = kq₁q₂/r with q₁ = +e and q₂ = −e. Dividing the energy in joules by e converts it to electron volts.
solution.why_others_wrong: +27.2 eV ignores the opposite signs of the charges. −13.6 eV is half of the potential energy (the total energy in Bohr's model), not the potential energy. −2.72 eV is an error of a factor of 10 in converting ångströms to metres.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential energy of a system of charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with air between its plates has capacitance C₀ and plate separation d. An uncharged metal slab of thickness d/2, of the same area as the plates, is inserted between them parallel to the plates without touching them. The capacitance becomes:

solution.concept: Conductor inside a capacitor
solution.explanation: The field inside the metal slab is zero, so the potential difference between the plates is set only by the air gaps, whose total thickness is d − d/2 = d/2, wherever the slab sits. The capacitor behaves as one with plate separation d/2.
steps: V = E₀(d − t) with t = d/2
solution.why_others_wrong: C₀ ignores the slab. C₀/2 treats the slab as increasing the separation. 4C₀ squares the effect.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', the parallel plate capacitor (with a conductor inside: field inside a conductor is zero)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electron with a kinetic energy of 100 eV enters a region of uniform electric field of 1000 V/m, moving in the same direction as the field. The distance it travels in the field before it momentarily comes to rest is:

solution.concept: Retardation of an electron by an electric field
solution.explanation: The force on an electron is opposite to the field, so an electron moving along the field is slowed down. It stops after climbing a potential difference equal to its kinetic energy in electron volts.
steps: Kinetic energy 100 eV → it can move against a potential difference of 100 V
In a field of 1000 V/m, 100 V corresponds to 100/1000 = 0.1 m = 10 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 cm and 1 m are errors of a factor of 10 in converting units. 20 cm doubles the distance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', relation between electric field and potential

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An uncharged metal sphere stands on an insulating stand. A negatively charged rod is brought near it without touching it. With the rod held there, the sphere is connected to the earth by a wire, and the wire is then removed. Finally the rod is taken away. The sphere is left with:

options.text: A negative charge spread uniformly over its surface
A positive charge spread uniformly over its surface
A positive charge confined to the side that was nearer the rod

solution.concept: Charging by induction
solution.explanation: The negative rod repels free electrons to the far side of the sphere, leaving the near side positive. Earthing lets those repelled electrons flow away to the earth. When the earth connection and then the rod are removed, the sphere has a deficit of electrons, a net positive charge, which spreads uniformly over the conducting surface.
steps: Rod near: electrons pushed to the far side
Earthing: those electrons go to the earth
Rod removed: net positive charge redistributes uniformly over the sphere
solution.why_others_wrong: Induction gives a charge opposite to that of the rod, so 'negative' is wrong. 'No net charge' forgets the electrons that left through the earth wire. Once the rod is removed, the charge on an isolated sphere spreads evenly; it does not stay on one side.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', charging by induction
solution.final_answer: Option C: A positive charge spread uniformly over its surface

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An electron released from rest in an electrostatic field moves towards the region of higher potential.
Reason (R): The force on a negative charge is opposite to the electric field, and the electric field points in the direction in which the potential decreases.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Motion of a negative charge in a potential gradient
solution.explanation: The field points from higher to lower potential. A negative charge experiences a force opposite to the field, i.e. towards higher potential, and starting from rest it moves that way, its potential energy (−e)V falling.
steps: F = −eE points along increasing V → the electron moves towards higher V
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the complete reason for A, so B is wrong; both are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', relation between electric field and potential
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.01 m² separated by 1 mm of air and is connected to a 100 V battery. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its capacitance is 88.5 pF.
(b) The charge on each plate has magnitude 8.85 nC.
(c) The electric field between the plates is 10⁵ V/m.
(d) The energy stored in the capacitor is 8.85 × 10⁻⁷ J.
(e) The surface charge density on each plate has magnitude 8.85 × 10⁻⁷ C/m².

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Parallel plate capacitor: C, Q, E, U and σ
solution.explanation: C = ε₀A/d, Q = CV, E = V/d, U = ½CV² and σ = Q/A.
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) uses CV² without the factor ½; every option containing (d) is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', the parallel plate capacitor and energy stored in a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, free charges in it move to its surfaces and make the field inside it zero, as happens in a conductor.
Statement II: A dielectric placed in an external electric field gets polarised through the displacement or reorientation of its bound charges, that is, of its molecular dipoles.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conductors versus dielectrics in an external field
solution.explanation: A dielectric has no free charges that can move through it. The field stretches non-polar molecules and partly aligns polar ones, giving a net dipole moment per unit volume. The resulting bound surface charges reduce the field inside the dielectric but do not cancel it.
steps: Statement I: describes a conductor, not a dielectric → false
Statement II: polarisation by bound charges → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, so only D fits.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', dielectrics and polarisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four identical point charges, each of +1 μC, are fixed at the corners of a square of side 0.3 m in air. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the magnitude of the net electrostatic force on any one of the charges is about:

solution.concept: Superposition of Coulomb forces
solution.explanation: The two neighbours at distance a push the charge along the two sides; their resultant lies along the diagonal. The charge at the opposite corner, at distance a√2, also pushes it along the diagonal.
steps: Two side forces at 90°: 0.1√2 ≈ 0.141 N along the diagonal
Diagonal charge: kq²/(2a²) = 0.05 N along the diagonal
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.14 N leaves out the charge at the opposite corner. 0.25 N adds the magnitudes of all three forces as if they were along one line. 0.21 N uses a√2 instead of (a√2)² for the diagonal force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', forces between multiple charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 2 μF capacitor and a 4 μF capacitor, each of which can safely withstand a potential difference of at most 100 V, are connected in series. The largest potential difference that can safely be applied across the series combination is:

solution.concept: Sharing of voltage in a series combination
solution.explanation: In series both capacitors carry the same charge, so the smaller capacitance takes the larger voltage (V = Q/C). The 2 μF capacitor reaches its limit first.
steps: Limit for 2 μF: Q = 2 μF × 100 V = 200 μC
Then V across 4 μF = 200 μC/4 μF = 50 V
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 V assumes both can be at 100 V together, which is impossible since they carry equal charges. 100 V wastes the 4 μF capacitor's share. 300 V lets the 4 μF capacitor reach 100 V, which would put 200 V across the 2 μF capacitor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', combination of capacitors (in series)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Twenty-seven identical spherical drops of mercury, each charged to the same potential V, coalesce to form a single large spherical drop. Taking the potential to be zero at infinity, the potential of the large drop is:

solution.concept: Potential of a charged conducting sphere, V = kQ/R
solution.explanation: Charge is conserved and so is the volume: the total charge is 27q, and 27 small spheres of radius r make one sphere of radius 3r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27V forgets that the radius also grows. 3V takes the radius to grow 9 times. V/3 inverts the radius ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential due to a point charge (charged conducting sphere)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An isolated conducting sphere of radius 9 cm in air carries a charge of 3 μC. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electrostatic energy stored in its field is:

solution.concept: Energy stored by a charged isolated conductor
solution.explanation: An isolated sphere has capacitance C = 4πε₀R, and the energy stored when it carries charge Q is Q²/(2C).
steps: Check: V = kQ/R = 3 × 10⁵ V and ½QV = 0.45 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.9 J leaves out the ½. 4.5 × 10⁻³ J keeps the radius in centimetres. 10 J computes kQ²/R², which is a force, not an energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', capacitors and capacitance; energy stored in a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Just outside the surface of a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field has magnitude σ/ε₀, which is twice the field σ/(2ε₀) of a large thin plane sheet carrying the same surface charge density σ.
Reason (R): Inside the conductor the field is zero, so all the flux through a small pillbox-shaped Gaussian surface drawn across the conductor's surface leaves through its outer face; for the thin sheet the flux leaves through both faces of the pillbox.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Gauss's law at a conductor's surface versus a sheet of charge
solution.explanation: For a pillbox of face area ΔS enclosing charge σΔS, Gauss's law gives total flux σΔS/ε₀. At a conductor the inner face lies in the conductor (E = 0), so E ΔS = σΔS/ε₀ → E = σ/ε₀. For the sheet the same flux is shared by two faces, 2EΔS = σΔS/ε₀ → E = σ/(2ε₀).
steps: Conductor: one face carries all the flux → σ/ε₀
Sheet: two faces share it → σ/(2ε₀)
solution.why_others_wrong: R is exactly the Gauss's-law reason for the factor of two, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', applications of Gauss's law; 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', electrostatics of conductors
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A point charge +q is placed at the centre of the cavity of a thick, uncharged, conducting spherical shell of inner radius a and outer radius b. In electrostatic equilibrium, which of the following statements are correct? (k = 1/(4πε₀); r is the distance from the centre.)

(a) A charge −q is induced on the inner surface of the shell.
(b) A charge +q appears on the outer surface of the shell.
(c) The electric field within the material of the shell (a < r < b) is zero.
(d) The electric field at a point outside the shell (r > b) has magnitude kq/r².
(e) The electric field everywhere inside the cavity (r < a) is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Gauss's law and conductors: induced charges
solution.explanation: In equilibrium the field in the conducting material is zero. A Gaussian sphere drawn inside the material then has zero flux, so it must enclose zero charge: the inner surface carries −q. The shell is neutral, so +q sits on the outer surface. Outside, a Gaussian sphere encloses q − q + q = q.
steps: (a) true: enclosed charge must be zero within the metal
(c) true: electrostatic field inside a conductor is zero
(e) false: the cavity contains the charge +q, so the field there is kq/r²
solution.why_others_wrong: The zero-field result for a cavity holds only when the cavity contains no charge, so (e) is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Gauss's law; 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', electrostatics of conductors
